headline: Belmar Rocks at Dawn: Blues Under the Bunker, Bass Gone to Ghosts
subhead: The bluefish blitz we predicted has arrived on the bunker schools, but the warm water pushed the stripers into a nighttime-only pattern up and down the jetty line.
body_markdown:
Five-fifteen this morning, Sea Bright rocks, and I'm standing next to a kid I'd never met who just buried a Hopkins into a bunker pod so thick it looked like the water had a rash. He didn't know what to do next — I did. Told him to let it sink on a semi-slack line and rip it up through the pod, and thirty seconds later he's got an 18-inch bluefish trying to remove his fingers. Welcome to jetty country in mid-July.

This is the bunker week we've been waiting on. Peanut and adult bunker schools have packed tight against the beach from Sea Bright down through Monmouth Beach and into Belmar, and the blues are stacked underneath them instead of chasing them offshore — which is exactly the mechanism I flagged you on last week. Warm surface water concentrates the bait against structure, predators quit burning calories chasing open water, and you get this: violent, compressed feeding right off the rocks. I've watched three straight mornings of blitzes at the north end of the Sea Bright jetty field, another one working off the Sandy Hook side of the inlet on the last two hours of the incoming. Poppers, Hopkins, anything chrome and heavy that you can throw through a bird-and-bunker ball — doesn't matter much. The blues aren't picky right now, they're just there in numbers, cocktail-to-mid-teens mostly, with the occasional 6-pounder mixed in that'll make your drag sing.

Here's the part that's not as fun to write. Stripers have gone dark on us — literally. Inshore water's sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off the buoy readings I trust, and that's enough to push bass off the daytime bite entirely. This isn't fish disappearing, it's fish doing what warm-blooded thinking predators do when the water gets uncomfortable: they retreat to deeper structure and current breaks and they feed at night. I worked the Manasquan Inlet rocks two hours before first light on Tuesday — dead calm, incoming tide just starting to build — and put two schoolies in the 26–28 inch range on a black Bomber long-A worked slow along the north jetty face. That's the program right now. If you want bass on this beat, you're getting up when everyone else is going to bed, or you're fishing the last gray hour before sunrise like I did. Shark River Inlet's producing the same way on the last of the outgoing — bunker chunks fished tight to the rocks on a fish-finder rig, 2 ounces of egg sinker, enough to hold bottom without getting swept. Don't expect a pile. Expect one or two quality fish if you put the time in and fish the tide correctly.

Fluke is the one bite you can set your watch by right now, and it's exactly where I told you it'd be heading — off the back bay mud and into the inlet mouths and the nearshore reef structure as that water kept climbing. Manasquan Inlet itself has been steady on the last two hours of the ebb, boats and shore guys both picking through keepers in the 18-to-20 inch range in 15 to 25 feet of water right off the rock pile, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged dead slow along bottom. Belmar's inlet edge has done the same on the same stage of tide. If you're working the jetty from shore, cast up-current and let the bucktail settle before you start the retrieve — these fish are holding tight to the rock seams where the current breaks, and a bait that swims past two feet off the structure gets ignored while one that ticks the rocks gets bit.

Blackfish and porgies are a summer afterthought on this stretch until the water turns again in the fall, so I'm not wasting your time on them this week. Worth knowing the porgies are still around the deeper stone at Manasquan and Shark River if you need bait-shop consolation fishing on a slow morning, but nobody's writing home about it.

Moon's building toward the first quarter on the 21st, which means the tides are easing off the spring push we had around the new moon — that's actually good news for the fluke bite, since a softer current lets the bucktail stay in the strike zone longer instead of getting swept through in two seconds. For the bass, I'd keep working the same nighttime program through the week: high tide around dawn on the incoming stages is when I've had the best luck, working plugs slow along jetty faces at Sea Bright, Manasquan, and the Spring Lake rocks. If the bunker schools hold and the weather stays calm — no reason right now to think they won't — expect the bluefish blitz to keep spreading south along Belmar and Asbury Park through the weekend. The minute a stiff onshore blow scatters that bait, this whole pattern resets, so if you've got a window in the next few days, I wouldn't wait on it.
